newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten warns of legal muddle ahead for Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Patten warns of legal muddle ahead for Hong Kong.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten warned on Sunday that Beijing's proposals to water down civil liberties could sow legal confusion in the post-1997 Hong Kong government.

A sub-committee of the Chinese-controlled body overseeing Hong Kong's return to Beijing's rule recommended last week that 25 of the territory's law be scrapped or amended, including part of its human rights bill.
The action sparked outrage in Hong Kong, which reverts to Chinese control at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British rule.
"What are some of the consequences of the Sub-Group's recommendations?" Patten said in a broadcast on government radio.
"One pretty obvious consequence is that the early months of the (post-1997) government will be dominated by legal arguments and courtroom battles," he added.
Patten challenged China's appointees to the provisional legislature -- which Beijing will install in place of the present elected chamber -- to explain how they could support China's plans.
"Those who have agreed to help close down Hong Kong's elected legislature can at least prevent the trashing of Hong Kong's civil liberties.
"Many of them actually voted for our Bill of Rights," he said. "Have they all changed their mind?"

Patten said the 60 members of the Provisional Legislature -- almost half of them members of the doomed legislature elected in 1995 under democratic reforms that he introduced -- had yet to explain the legal justification for watering down the laws.
"I think there's one very simple question which has to be addressed.
"Is Hong Kong going to have the same freedoms after 1997 -- yes or no?
"If the answer to that question is yes, then why, I repeat, do we need to make all these changes?

"And if the answer is no, we are entitled to learn just what is going to be usurped, just how much is going to be taken away, why that's going to happen and how it squares with the international covenants and all the other promises China has made."
China has argued the changes will not weaken civil liberties in Hong Kong after the handover.
